lessons.title: Study Session 1: A System You Can Actually Find Things In

blocks.text: Introduction Domingas Sequeira could once find any document in her office within a minute, because she alone had built the system and kept it entirely in her head. When she took two weeks of leave, her colleagues could not find a single contract without calling her. This session teaches you to build a filing and records system that works for whoever needs it, not only for the person who built it. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why undocumented, ad hoc filing habits fail as records grow. Distinguish an active record from one ready for archiving or disposal. Apply a consistent classification structure. Maintain a record's authenticity and integrity over time. Audit an existing filing system for gaps. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A System That Only Worked for One Person Domingas Sequeira manages administrative operations for a construction consultancy in Luanda, and for three years she organized contracts, invoices and correspondence using a private logic that made sense only to her, folders named after her own private shorthand, documents saved wherever there happened to be space. When she took two weeks of medical leave, a colleague covering for her spent an entire afternoon searching for a single signed contract that Domingas could have found in under a minute. 2.2 A Standard Built for Records That Outlive Any One Person ISO 15489-1:2016, Information and Documentation, Records Management, Part 1: Concepts and Principles, published by the International Organization for Standardization, sets out principles for creating, capturing and controlling records so they remain usable regardless of who created them or who needs them later. Its central point is that a record's value depends on four essential characteristics, authenticity, reliability, usability and integrity, maintained consistently through a defined lifecycle, from creation through active use to eventual archiving or disposal, rather than through the private memory of whoever happens to manage it. 2.3 Building a System Anyone Can Use Naming a Consistent Classification Structure Organizing records by a shared, logical structure, project, client, or document type, rather than by private shorthand, means any authorized person can locate what they need without asking the one person who built the system. Distinguishing Active Records From Ones Ready to Archive A record still needed for daily reference belongs in an active system; one no longer needed daily but still required for a defined retention period belongs in an archive, and treating every record identically, regardless of how often it is used, clutters the system that matters most. Protecting a Record's Authenticity and Integrity Keeping an original document intact, dated and traceable to who created or last modified it protects its value as genuine evidence, which matters far beyond simple convenience. 2.4 Key Practices Organize records by a shared, logical structure rather than private shorthand. Distinguish active records from those ready for archiving or disposal. Keep records traceable to who created or last modified them. Review a filing system periodically for gaps or drift back into ad hoc habits. 2.5 A Worked Example: Domingas's Rebuilt System After the missed contract, Domingas rebuilt her filing system around three shared categories, active client, archived client, and internal administration, each divided consistently by year and document type, with a one-page guide explaining the structure posted where any colleague could find it. Six months later, when Domingas took another period of leave, a colleague located a needed insurance document within minutes, without a single phone call. The documents themselves had not changed. The system around them had. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Building a filing system around private shorthand that only its creator can navigate is the mistake that eventually costs an office the most time, because the system's apparent efficiency for one person becomes a genuine liability the moment that person is unavailable. A system nobody else can use is not really a system at all. 2.7 A System That Outlasts Its Builder Domingas's filing system did not become more complicated once she rebuilt it around shared logic. It became something the whole office could actually rely on, whether or not she happened to be the one looking for a document that day. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to build a filing and records system around shared, consistent structure rather than private memory. This prepares you for Study Session 2, where the same discipline shapes how you manage a calendar that other people also depend on.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Look at a system you currently use to organize documents. Could a colleague navigate it without asking you? 2. Name one change you could make to your own filing system to make it usable by someone other than you. Practical Output: Practical Output A one-page filing structure guide naming shared categories for active, archived and internal records, usable by someone other than its creator. 7.0 References and Further Reading ISO 15489-1:2016. Information and Documentation, Records Management, Part 1: Concepts and Principles. Geneva: International Organization for Standardization. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 24:3-4, on a house built by wisdom and its rooms filled through knowledge. Qur'an, Surah An-Nisa 4:58, on rendering trusts to those to whom they are due.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Whose Calendar Is It, Really

blocks.text: Introduction Ferdinand Okemba's calendar filled itself every single day with whoever asked first, until the one task that actually mattered most, a quarterly budget review, kept sliding to next week, then the week after. This session teaches you to manage a calendar according to what actually matters, not simply whoever asks loudest or first. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Distinguish urgent from important when scheduling. Protect time for important, non-urgent work. Negotiate competing calendar requests from multiple stakeholders. Build in buffer time for the unexpected. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Calendar Full, and Still Behind Ferdinand Okemba coordinates scheduling for a regional trade office in Brazzaville, managing calendars for three senior staff as well as his own. His days filled reliably with requests, an urgent phone call here, an impromptu meeting there, and the quarterly budget review he had been asked to prepare kept sliding, week after week, because nothing about it ever felt as urgent as whatever had just landed in his inbox. 2.2 Urgent and Important Are Not the Same Thing In 1989, Stephen Covey published The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, introducing a time management matrix that sorts tasks along two dimensions, urgency and importance, rather than urgency alone. Tasks that are both urgent and important demand immediate attention. Tasks that are important but not urgent, like long-term planning, rarely announce themselves loudly and are easiest to keep postponing. Covey's central point is that effective scheduling deliberately protects time for this important, non-urgent category, because it is exactly the work most likely to be crowded out by whatever feels urgent in the moment. 2.3 Scheduling According to What Matters Sorting a Request by Urgency and Importance, Not Urgency Alone Asking, of any new request, whether it is actually important as well as urgent, prevents a calendar from filling entirely with whatever simply arrived first or loudest. Protecting Time for Important, Non-Urgent Work Blocking specific time for work that matters but does not announce itself urgently, and treating that block as seriously as any other appointment, is what keeps it from being crowded out indefinitely. Negotiating Competing Requests Openly When two stakeholders want the same time slot, naming the conflict directly and asking each what flexibility they actually have produces a better outcome than silently favouring whoever asked first. 2.4 Key Practices Sort new requests by both urgency and importance, not urgency alone. Block specific time for important, non-urgent work, and protect that block. Name scheduling conflicts openly rather than resolving them silently. Build buffer time into a calendar for the unexpected, rather than scheduling back to back. 2.5 A Worked Example: Ferdinand's Protected Block Ferdinand began blocking two hours every Tuesday morning specifically for the quarterly budget review, marked on the shared calendar as unavailable, the same way he would mark an external meeting. When a colleague tried to book that slot for a routine check-in, Ferdinand named the conflict directly and offered an alternative time later that day. The budget review was completed on schedule for the first time in three quarters, not because Ferdinand's days became any less busy, but because the one thing that actually mattered most finally had a place on the calendar that nothing else was allowed to quietly take. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating every incoming request as equally urgent, and filling a calendar in the order requests happen to arrive, is the habit that lets the most important work slide indefinitely without ever being explicitly postponed. A calendar can look completely full and still contain almost none of what actually matters most. 2.7 A Calendar That Reflects What Matters Ferdinand's calendar did not become emptier once he began protecting time for important work. It became a more honest reflection of what actually mattered, rather than a record of whoever happened to ask first each day. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to schedule according to both urgency and importance, protecting time for what matters most. This prepares you for Study Session 3, where the same discipline supports coordinating the many moving parts of a meeting or event.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Name one important but non-urgent task on your own plate that keeps sliding. Why does it keep sliding? 2. Block a specific period this week for that task, and name what you will do if something tries to take that slot. Practical Output: Practical Output One protected calendar block for an important, non-urgent task, with a plan for how to respond if a competing request tries to take that time. 7.0 References and Further Reading Covey, S.R. (1989). The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People. New York: Simon & Schuster. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Ecclesiastes 3:1, on there being a season and a time for every matter under heaven. Qur'an, Surah Al-Asr 103:1-3, on time, and those who do not lose out being the ones who use it well.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Nothing Falls Through at the Event Itself

blocks.text: Introduction Afi Lawson, who cares for her aging mother most evenings after work, had coordinated dozens of successful events from memory, until the one week her mother had a health scare, and the catering order for a fifty-person conference was never actually placed. A specific, written checklist, not a sharper memory, is what this session offers as the real protection against exactly that kind of gap. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why complex, multi-step coordination tasks benefit from a checklist. Build a checklist covering venue, invitations, materials and catering. Distinguish a checklist from a vague mental list. Use a checklist under real-time pressure. Revise a checklist after something is missed. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 The One Detail Memory Didn't Hold Afi Lawson coordinates internal events for a telecommunications company in Lome, and for two years she managed venue bookings, invitations, materials and catering for every major meeting entirely from memory and experience, without a single written checklist. The week her mother had a serious health scare, Afi's attention was, understandably, elsewhere, and the catering order for a fifty-person quarterly conference was never placed. The gap was discovered an hour before the event began. 2.2 What a Simple Checklist Actually Prevents In 2009, the surgeon and writer Atul Gawande published The Checklist Manifesto, drawing on real research, including work by physician Peter Pronovost, whose simple five-step checklist for inserting central lines in intensive care units cut a hospital's infection rate from eleven percent to near zero within months. Gawande's central point, drawn from that and other examples across aviation, construction and business, is that even highly skilled, experienced people reliably miss steps in complex, multi-step tasks under pressure, and a specific, written checklist catches exactly the kind of omission that memory alone, however capable, eventually lets through. 2.3 Building and Using a Real Checklist Writing Down Every Actual Step, Not a Vague Mental List A checklist that says confirm catering is far less useful than one that says confirm catering order, quantity and delivery time by a named date; specificity is what makes a checklist catch a gap a vague mental list would miss. Covering Every Category a Coordination Task Actually Involves A complete event checklist names venue, invitations, materials and catering as separate categories, each with its own specific steps, rather than treating the whole event as one undifferentiated task. Using the Checklist Even When Time Is Short A checklist is most valuable exactly when time is tightest and memory is most likely to fail; skipping it under pressure removes the one safeguard built for precisely that situation. 2.4 Key Practices Write specific steps on a checklist, not a vague mental list of categories. Cover venue, invitations, materials and catering as distinct categories. Use the checklist every time, especially under time pressure. Revise a checklist immediately after anything is missed, so the same gap cannot recur. Share the checklist so someone else could use it if you are unavailable. 2.5 A Worked Example: Afi's Rebuilt Process After the catering gap, Afi built a written checklist with four sections, venue, invitations, materials, catering, each broken into specific dated steps: confirm venue capacity two weeks prior, send invitations ten days prior, confirm catering order and delivery time five days prior, print materials two days prior. Three months later, a similar family emergency pulled her attention away again, days before another major event. This time, a colleague picked up Afi's written checklist, followed it step by step, and the event ran without incident. The checklist did not depend on Afi's memory being available that week. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Relying entirely on memory and experience for complex, multi-step coordination, without ever writing the steps down, is the habit that eventually fails even the most capable coordinator, usually at the exact moment attention is pulled elsewhere by something equally real. A checklist is not a sign of inexperience. It is what protects experienced work from an ordinary, human lapse. 2.7 A Safeguard, Not a Crutch Afi still coordinates events the same way she always has, from long experience and a genuine feel for what a room needs. The difference now is that none of it depends on her memory alone holding up on the one week it happens to be pulled elsewhere. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to write and use a specific checklist that protects complex event and meeting coordination from ordinary lapses in memory. This prepares you for Study Session 4, where the same attention to detail shapes how you manage office supplies and vendor relationships.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a coordination task you usually manage from memory. What is the one detail most likely to slip if your attention were pulled elsewhere? 2. Write a specific, dated checklist for one upcoming event or meeting you are responsible for. Practical Output: Practical Output One written, specific checklist for an upcoming meeting or event, covering venue, invitations, materials and catering with dated steps. 7.0 References and Further Reading Gawande, A. (2009). The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right. New York: Metropolitan Books. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 1 Corinthians 14:40, on all things being done decently and in order. Qur'an, Surah Yusuf 12:47-48, on Yusuf's advice to store grain in preparation for the years ahead.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Knowing Which Supplier Actually Matters

blocks.text: Introduction Mamadou Camara spent as much time negotiating the price of printer paper as he spent managing the single supplier his entire operation depended on for specialized parts, until a shortage from that one critical supplier nearly halted production for a week. This session teaches you to tell the difference between a routine purchase and a critical one, and to manage each accordingly. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Distinguish low-risk, routine purchases from high-risk, high-impact ones. Categorize a purchase or supplier by profit impact and supply risk. Apply a different vendor management approach to each category. Avoid treating every vendor relationship identically. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Equal Attention, Unequal Stakes Mamadou Camara manages procurement for a manufacturing operation in Conakry, and for years he applied the same negotiating effort and attention to every purchase, office supplies, cleaning services, and the specialized replacement parts his machinery depended on, treating each vendor relationship as equally important. When the sole supplier of one critical part experienced a shortage, Mamadou had no backup relationship in place, and production slowed for nearly a week. 2.2 Not Every Purchase Carries the Same Risk In 1983, Peter Kraljic published Purchasing Must Become Supply Management in the Harvard Business Review, introducing a matrix that categorizes purchases along two dimensions, their impact on profit and the risk involved in supplying them. Routine, low-risk items need only efficient processing. High-impact but low-risk items benefit from negotiating leverage. Low-impact but high-risk items need a secure, simplified supply arrangement. High-impact, high-risk items, Kraljic's strategic category, require close, actively managed supplier relationships, because a disruption there carries the most serious consequences. 2.3 Managing Differently, Deliberately Categorizing a Purchase by Impact and Risk, Not Habit Asking, of each significant purchase, how much it actually affects operations and how risky its supply actually is, rather than managing every purchase the same way out of habit, reveals where real attention belongs. Applying the Right Approach to Each Category A routine, low-risk purchase deserves efficient, low-effort processing; a high-impact, high-risk purchase deserves a genuinely managed relationship, backup options, and regular check-ins, not the same brief transaction applied to both. Building Redundancy Where Risk Is Highest For the purchases that matter most and carry the most supply risk, identifying at least one backup supplier in advance protects against exactly the kind of disruption that catches an office unprepared. 2.4 Key Practices Categorize significant purchases by their impact on operations and their supply risk. Apply efficient, low-effort processing to routine, low-risk purchases. Give high-impact, high-risk purchases a genuinely managed relationship with backup options. Review your vendor categories periodically, since risk and impact can shift over time. 2.5 A Worked Example: Mamadou's Recategorized Suppliers After the shortage, Mamadou reviewed every significant supplier against Kraljic's two dimensions. Office supplies and general cleaning services were genuinely low-risk and low-impact, and Mamadou simplified their ordering process to require minimal ongoing attention. The specialized parts supplier was clearly high-impact and high-risk, and Mamadou began a formal quarterly relationship review with that supplier, plus identified and qualified a second backup supplier for the same part. Eight months later, when the primary supplier again faced a delay, Mamadou activated the backup relationship within a day, and production was not affected at all. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating every vendor relationship with equal attention and effort, regardless of its actual impact and risk, is the habit that leaves the most critical relationships under-managed while routine ones absorb time they don't actually need. Equal attention is not the same as appropriate attention. 2.7 Attention Where It Actually Matters Mamadou's procurement work did not become more time-consuming after he categorized his suppliers. It became better distributed, with real attention finally going to the relationships where a disruption would actually matter most. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to categorize purchases and suppliers by their impact and risk, and to manage each category differently. This prepares you for Study Session 5, where the same discipline of sorting things correctly shapes how you process incoming correspondence and documents.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Name one purchase or supplier relationship in your own work. Is it routine, or does a disruption there carry real risk? 2. For one high-impact, high-risk purchase you rely on, name a backup option you could identify or qualify. Practical Output: Practical Output A short categorization of three real purchases or supplier relationships by impact and risk, with a management approach named for each. 7.0 References and Further Reading Kraljic, P. (1983). Purchasing must become supply management. Harvard Business Review, 61(5), 109 to 117. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 27:23, on knowing well the condition of your flocks and giving attention to your herds. Hadith, Sunan al-Tirmidhi, on tying your camel and trusting in Allah, on taking practical precaution alongside faith.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Getting It Out of Your Head and Into a System

blocks.text: Introduction Nazare Fonseca, who has dyslexia and has built her own careful systems for working with written text, found that the real problem in her office was not reading any single document, it was the growing pile of unprocessed correspondence sitting in her mind at once, each one only half attended to. This session teaches you to get incoming correspondence out of your head and into a reliable system, so nothing has to be held in memory at all. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why unprocessed, uncaptured tasks create ongoing mental strain. Capture incoming correspondence into a single reliable system rather than memory. Clarify what each item actually requires. Route each item to its correct destination. Distinguish processing from doing. Close the loop once an item is handled. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Mind Full of Half-Finished Items Nazare Fonseca handles incoming correspondence for a shipping agency in Praia, and for months she kept a running mental list of every email, letter and form that needed a response, revisiting the same unfinished items repeatedly throughout each day without ever fully processing any of them. She was not struggling to read the documents themselves, careful strategies she had built over years handled that well. She was struggling because dozens of unprocessed items sat, unresolved, taking up space in her attention at once. 2.2 Why Unfinished Items Occupy the Mind In 1927, the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik published a study, conducted under the Gestalt theorist Kurt Lewin, finding that people remember and mentally revisit unfinished or interrupted tasks far more persistently than completed ones. Her research, beginning with an observation of waiters who remembered orders only until they were served, showed that an unfinished task creates a kind of mental tension that persists until the task is either completed or deliberately released, which is exactly what keeps an unprocessed item resurfacing in a person's attention long after it first arrived. 2.3 Capturing, Clarifying and Routing Capturing Everything Into One Reliable System Writing every incoming item down in a single trusted place the moment it arrives, rather than trying to hold it in memory, releases the mental tension an unfinished item otherwise creates. Clarifying What Each Item Actually Requires Deciding, for each captured item, exactly what action it requires, a reply, a forward, a filed record, turns a vague pile of correspondence into a set of specific, resolvable tasks. Routing Each Item to Its Correct Destination, Then Closing the Loop Sending each item to wherever it actually needs to go, and marking it as handled once it arrives there, closes the mental loop Zeigarnik's research describes, freeing attention for whatever comes next. 2.4 Key Practices Capture every incoming item into one single, trusted system the moment it arrives. Clarify exactly what action each item actually requires. Route each item to its correct destination rather than leaving it in a general pile. Distinguish processing an item, deciding what it needs, from actually doing that action. Mark an item as closed once it has been fully handled. 2.5 A Worked Example: Nazare's Single System Nazare built one simple intake log, every incoming item recorded the moment it arrived, along with what it required and where it was headed. She set aside twenty minutes each morning purely for processing, deciding what each new item needed, without necessarily completing the action itself in that same sitting. Within two weeks, the mental exhaustion of tracking dozens of half-finished items had genuinely eased, not because she was completing tasks any faster, but because nothing sat unprocessed and unrecorded, quietly occupying her attention throughout the day. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Trying to hold every incoming item in memory, revisiting the same unprocessed correspondence repeatedly without ever fully deciding what it requires, is the habit that exhausts even careful, capable people at this stage. An item does not need to be finished to stop occupying the mind. It only needs to be captured and clearly assigned somewhere reliable. 2.7 Out of the Head, Into the System Nazare's inbox did not become smaller the week she built her intake log. Her mind did, freed from holding dozens of unprocessed items that a reliable system could now hold instead. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to capture, clarify and route incoming correspondence into a reliable system, rather than holding it in memory. This closes the operational core of the course and prepares you for Study Session 6, where you will prioritize among everything that reliable system surfaces.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Name one task or piece of correspondence you have been mentally revisiting without fully processing. What would capturing it look like? 2. Set aside twenty minutes this week purely to process, not complete, everything currently sitting unresolved in your attention. Practical Output: Practical Output One single intake log capturing at least five real pending items, each with a clarified action and a named destination. 7.0 References and Further Reading Zeigarnik, B. (1927). On finished and unfinished tasks. Psychologische Forschung, 9, 1 to 85. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Matthew 11:28, on coming to find rest for those who labor and are heavy laden. Qur'an, Surah At-Talaq 65:2-3, on Allah making a way out and providing for whoever is mindful of Him.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Deciding What Actually Goes First

blocks.text: Introduction Amira Chebbi, raising her son alone while managing the front office of a busy legal practice in Tunis, prided herself on handling five things at once, until she realized how often that constant switching left small, costly errors behind, a misfiled document here, a missed call there. This final session asks you to bring every earlier session together into the discipline of prioritizing deliberately, rather than switching constantly between everything at once. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why rapid task switching carries a real cognitive cost. Distinguish genuine multitasking from rapid switching between single tasks. Sequence competing administrative demands deliberately. Protect focused blocks of time from interruption. Recognise when to say a task must wait. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Proud of Doing Five Things at Once Amira Chebbi manages the front office of a legal practice in Tunis, and for years she considered her ability to juggle phone calls, scheduling, filing and visitor requests simultaneously to be one of her strongest skills. A careful audit of one particularly busy week, prompted by a client complaint about a missed callback, revealed a pattern she had not noticed: the more she switched rapidly between tasks, the more small errors, a misfiled document, a missed message, quietly accumulated. 2.2 What Task Switching Actually Costs In 2001, the researchers Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans published a study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology examining what happens when people rapidly switch between different tasks rather than completing one before starting the next. Their finding was clear: rapid task switching carries a measurable time cost and increases errors, and what feels like efficient multitasking is usually rapid switching between single tasks, with none of them receiving full attention, rather than genuine simultaneous processing. 2.3 Sequencing Deliberately Instead of Switching Constantly Recognising Switching for What It Actually Is Noticing that handling five things at once usually means rapidly alternating between them, not truly doing them simultaneously, is the first step toward sequencing tasks more deliberately. Sequencing Competing Demands on Purpose Deciding, briefly, which of several pending demands genuinely needs to happen first, rather than reacting to whichever one interrupts loudest, reduces the errors that rapid switching tends to produce. Protecting Focused Blocks From Interruption Setting aside short, protected periods for tasks that require real attention, and treating interruptions during that block as things to note and address afterward, produces more accurate work than handling everything as it arrives. 2.4 Key Practices Recognise that handling several things at once usually means rapid switching, not true simultaneous processing. Sequence competing demands deliberately rather than reacting to whichever interrupts loudest. Protect short, focused blocks of time from interruption for tasks that need real attention. Say clearly when a task must wait, rather than switching to it immediately out of habit. Review where errors actually occur to see whether switching is the real cause. 2.5 A Worked Example: Amira's Sequenced Morning After the audit, Amira restructured her morning into short, sequenced blocks: fifteen minutes for phone messages, then a protected twenty-minute block for scheduling with her phone set to voicemail, then a return to messages and visitor requests. Genuine emergencies still interrupted her immediately. Routine requests waited, clearly and calmly, for their designated block. Within a month, the same kind of audit that had first revealed her error pattern showed a clear drop in misfiled documents and missed messages, not because Amira was working harder, but because she was finally giving each task a real, uninterrupted turn rather than switching between all of them at once. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating rapid switching between many tasks as equivalent to skilled multitasking is the assumption that quietly produces the most administrative errors, because switching itself carries a real, measurable cost that accumulates unnoticed across a busy day. Being constantly busy with everything is not the same as actually being effective at any of it. 2.7 A Turn for Everything, Rather Than a Little of Everything at Once Amira's office did not become quieter once she began sequencing her work deliberately. It became more accurate, because each task finally received a real, focused turn instead of a fraction of attention shared unevenly across everything at once, which is the same discipline, deciding deliberately what actually goes first, that every earlier session in this course has been building toward. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to sequence competing administrative demands deliberately, recognising the real cost of rapid task switching. This closes Course 91 and prepares you for Course 92, Digital Tools and Systems for the Modern Office.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a recent error in your own work. Could rapid switching between tasks have contributed to it? 2. Sequence tomorrow morning into two or three short, protected blocks for your most demanding tasks. Practical Output: Practical Output One sequenced plan for a busy period, naming protected blocks for demanding tasks and a rule for when an interruption must wait. 7.0 References and Further Reading Rubinstein, J.S., Meyer, D.E., & Evans, J.E. (2001). Executive control of cognitive processes in task switching. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 27(4), 763 to 797. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 4:25-27, on letting your eyes look directly forward and not swerving to the right or the left. Qur'an, Surah Luqman 31:19, on being moderate in one's pace.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: What happened when Mamadou's sole critical parts supplier experienced a shortage?
options: Nothing; a backup supplier was already in place
Production slowed for nearly a week because no backup relationship existed
